This is a complex issue that can't really be summed up with a simple yes or no answer. The short answer would be "no", but I'll expand on it anyway.

I live in Canada, which is a country that prides itself on it's diversity and tolerance. Being "Canadian" is simply a matter of being a citizen, birthplace is really irrelevant. There IS racism here, toward immigrants, natives, and French Canadians. The Quebecers can get quite twitchy about non-French too, causing a fair bit of racism themselves. But despite that, when some Muslim women faced some racist comments while riding the subway in Toronto, our nation responded with the #ILLRIDEWITHYOU hashtag, responding to racism with a display of hospitality and acceptance.

In a way, America is the same. Black culture is such a massive and inseparable part of America - from motown and James Dean, to hip hop and Michael Jackson. Some of the biggest icons in black culture are white, and some of the biggest icons in white culture are black. Black and white grew up with eachother in America like siblings growing up in the same house.

But just like Canada, there is racism in the USA too. From the KKK to the neo nazis, to the treatment of Japanese Americans, to more modern black on white racism. Racism definitely exists in America, just like murder, violence, and all the other tragedies in life.

Answering a question like "Is America Racist" requires that we first decide what qualifies a country as racist. Since it can be reasonably assumed that no country is completely without racism, that it exists to some extent or another in every country, we can rule out the qualification that "not racist" should be interpreted as "there are no instances of racism". So whether a country is racist or not can only be established by asking how much it pervades a nation at every level, and what direction it's moving in, as in, is it making an improvement or getting worse?

For how racism pervades a country, one has to consider now we find that all people are on an essentially equal legal footing, there is still socioeconomic segregation on top of a bunch of other issues. Black communities tend to be poorer, and have higher crime rates. The television networks and news media sources are in many cases showing signs of veiled racism. Not just black people, but many non-whites and ethnic minorities have reported that they are treated unfavorably as a result of their race. Many white people have also reported that they are treated unfavorably because of their race too, particularly at the hands of well-meaning but poorly executed schemes like affirmative action. There is also without doubt a huge cultural issue within law enforcement when it comes to racism. So I have to conclude that although America is vastly better than where it was, racism is still a pretty big issue. Detroit, after all, is a place that exists.

As for what direction it's headed in, one only has to peer back into history to see how far it's come. There's no doubt about it, America has been marching toward racial equality for well over a century. Some of the most famous figures in the history of racial equality movements have been Americans. There have been many very well loved non-white celebrities, too many to list, which shows how despite the fact that there is a seemingly booming market for racist news, there's an even bigger multi-billion dollar entertainment industry that's far more racially diverse and tolerant.

So weighing up those two points, we can conclude that although America is still a long way from being done with it's struggle against racism, it also has some of the worlds greatest examples of what happens when we all get along. It is at once both the knight and the dragon.
